annotations.keyFindings: Catheter draws haemolysed in 19.6 percent and venepuncture samples in 4.2 percent among 620 adult emergency samples; smaller catheters haemolysed more.
annotations.limitations: Method chosen by clinical situation; difficult access not accounted for; one department.

annotations.keyFindings: With a low-vacuum tube or small syringe, catheter samples haemolysed in 3.9 percent and venepuncture samples in 3.1 percent (difference 0.8 points, 95 percent CI -1.4 to 3.0).
annotations.limitations: Trained research nurses only; 260 patients; may not reflect routine practice.

annotations.keyFindings: Haemolysis was 2.0 percent for hand-carried and 5.6 percent for high-speed pneumatic tube samples, falling to 2.4 percent at a lower speed.
Pooled odds ratio 3.4 (95 percent CI 2.1 to 5.5) across 24 studies with I-squared 88 percent; smaller effects with low-vacuum tubes, syringes and trained collectors.
annotations.limitations: Mostly non-randomised studies at high risk of bias; varied haemolysis definitions.

annotations.keyFindings: In 410 paediatric samples, haemolysis was 11 percent with catheter draws, 7 percent with venepuncture and 16 percent with capillary samples.
annotations.limitations: Conference abstract without a date, methods or full paper; method quality not assessed.

annotations.keyFindings: Haemolysis was 2.1 percent for phlebotomists, 7.8 percent for nurses and 9.6 percent for physicians; nurse training was followed by 4.4 percent.
annotations.limitations: Role and method confounded; training coincided with a tube supplier change.

annotations.keyFindings: Across 1.2 million samples, haemolysis was 6.9 percent in emergency and 1.8 percent in inpatient samples; laboratory data could not identify catheter draws.
annotations.limitations: Collection method not recorded; site-level rates only.

annotations.keyFindings: Recommends site-level monitoring, analyser indices and collector training, and makes no recommendation on catheter draws because the evidence conflicts.

claims.text: In adult emergency patients, catheter draws haemolysed in 19.6 percent of samples and venepuncture in 4.2 percent, with method chosen by clinical situation.
claims.passage: Haemolysis, defined as a haemolysis index above the analyser's rejection threshold, occurred in 19.6 percent of catheter draws and 4.2 percent of venepuncture samples.
claims.interpretation: A large difference, but confounded by who needed a catheter.

claims.text: When catheter samples were drawn with a low-vacuum tube or small syringe in random order with venepuncture, haemolysis was 3.9 against 3.1 percent, a difference of 0.8 points.
claims.passage: Haemolysis occurred in 3.9 percent of catheter samples and 3.1 percent of venepuncture samples, a difference of 0.8 percentage points
claims.interpretation: Technique may remove most of the excess, at least with trained collectors.

claims.text: Whether drawing through a peripheral catheter raises haemolysis enough to justify a venepuncture policy is uncertain: estimates range from several-fold to almost no difference, and the size of the excess appears to depend on technique and collector training.
claims.passage: The effect was smaller in studies using low-vacuum tubes or syringes and in studies with trained collectors.
claims.interpretation: The conflict is probably explained by technique and collector, which a review with subgroups can examine; no policy should rest on a single study.

claims.text: High-speed pneumatic tube transport raised haemolysis from 2.0 to 5.6 percent, and a lower speed brought it to 2.4 percent.
claims.passage: Haemolysis above the rejection threshold occurred in 2.0 percent of hand-carried samples and 5.6 percent of samples sent at the high speed setting.
claims.interpretation: Transport confounds any comparison of emergency and ward samples.

claims.text: Laboratory information system data showed site-level differences (6.9 against 1.8 percent) but could not identify catheter draws, so they cannot estimate the effect of collection method.
claims.passage: The data could not identify whether samples were drawn through a catheter, so the effect of collection method could not be estimated.
claims.interpretation: The local retrospective option cannot answer the method question, because the local system does not record method either.

synthesis: Eight retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; one is an undated conference abstract whose method quality cannot be assessed. The evidence on catheter draws conflicts: a non-randomised emergency study found 19.6 against 4.2 percent haemolysis, a randomised crossover study with low-vacuum tubes or syringes found almost no difference, and a meta-analysis of 24 mostly non-randomised studies reported a pooled odds ratio of 3.4 with very high heterogeneity that shrank with better technique and trained collectors. Transport speed and collector role each change haemolysis and are entangled with collection method in routine data. Laboratory information system data show site differences but cannot identify catheter draws. A consensus group declined to recommend for or against catheter draws. The conflict is plausibly explained by technique, but the certainty of any single estimate is very low.
gradeRationale: Mostly non-randomised comparisons at high risk of bias, very high inconsistency across studies, and indirectness from trained research collectors; only one small randomised study. Certainty that catheter draws themselves raise haemolysis in routine practice is very low.
summary: Eight retrieved records appraised; the evidence conflicts; claim c3 records the conflict with high uncertainty; overall certainty very low.
